#805. Hunger Games Author Suzanne Collins Makes Rare Public Statement

Nearly 20 years after writing The Hunger Games, Suzanne Collins shared her opinion of Sunrise on the Reaping, the prequel movie of her OG series that starred Jennifer Lawrence and Woody Harrelson.

The odds were in Suzanne Collins' favor when filmmakers adapted her latest book.

After all, the Hunger Games author—who lives out of the spotlight, without social media—broke her cover to give her review of the series' upcoming prequel movie Sunrise on the Reaping. And even though she was not a producer on the film, she believes that their elaborate creative process behind adapting her 2025 prequel book for the screen felt like a tribute to the fantasy world she started 20 years ago.

"I could not be more excited for you to see The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," Collins said in a message to her fans Nov. 13, shared to the movie’s Instagram. "Director Francis Lawrence and company have put the finishing touches on a vibrant and devastating adaptation of the novel, leaving me with the happy job of singing its praises."

And in recounting the making of Haymitch Abernathy's origin story before the original trilogy, the 64-year-old couldn't help but praise Woody Harrelson's reprisal of the beloved character as well as Joseph Zada, who plays his younger counterpart in the movie.

"I can’t say enough about his masterful depiction of Haymitch in the original films," Collins said of Harrelson, adding that the cast was "led by a remarkably powerful and moving performance by Joseph Zada."

In addition, the writer applauded how the Zombieland star's return alongside original cast members Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson brought "such poignancy to the film," as together their characters "bridge Haymitch’s Hunger Games to Katniss’s tale."

Meanwhile, she said that the entire ensemble—including Elle Fanning and Ralph Fiennes—exceeded her expectations.

As Collins put it, "Gems, every last one. I truly can’t imagine a better cast."

But fans have more than the movie's stars to thank for the finished product. Collins—who has sat out the press tour for Sunrise on the Reaping following her last public appearance three years ago—also lauded the entire creative team from the screenwriters to the set designers, as well as singer Noah Kahan, who wrote one of the movie's emotional original songs, "Draw You Out."

And with that said, the Catching Fire scribe finished her letter by thanking her readers who made all five of her novels bestsellers.

"I feel such deep appreciation for your continued presence in Panem," she told her fans, before signing off, "May the odds be EVER in your favor!"

Before stepping back into the Capitol, keep reading for an inside look at Sunrise on the Reaping before its Nov. 20 premiere.

When Does The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping Hit Theaters?

A little birdie, er mockingjay, revealed the movie will be released November 20, 2026.

What Is The Hunger Games Book Sunrise on the Reaping About?

This book is a prequel to The Hunger Games and takes place 24 years prior to when readers first met Katniss Everdeen.The story opens on the morning of the reaping (the event where tributes from each district are chosen to compete) of the 50th Hunger Games (a.k.a. the Second Quarter Quell)."As the day dawns on the fiftieth annual Hunger Games, fear grips the districts of Panem," the description on author Suzanne Collins' website reads. "This year, in honor of the Quarter Quell, twice as many tributes will be taken from their homes. Back in District 12, Haymitch Abernathy is trying not to think too hard about his chances. All he cares about is making it through the day and being with the girl he loves."

Taking on the lead role of District 12 tribute Haymitch Abernathy is Joseph Zada. In the earlier Hunger Games movies, this part was played by Woody Harrelson.However, this isn't the first time fans have seen Joseph on their screens. The actor's past credits include We Were Liars, Invisible Boys, Total Control and The Speedway Murders.

Whitney Peak is playing Haymitch's girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird.Over the years, the actress has appeared in TV shows like the Gossip Girl revival, Home Before Dark and Chilling Adventures of Sabrina as well as in movies, including Campfire Kiss, Molly's Game and Hocus Pocus 2.

Mckenna Grace Takes on Role of Maysilee Donner

Gracing the screen as fellow District 12 tribute Maysilee Donner is Mckenna Grace.Fans have watched the actress grow up onscreen through her appearances on the Disney sitcom Crash & Bernstein, the soap opera The Young and the Restless and the film Gifted (her performance earning her a Critics Choice Award).Also among her lengthy list of credits are movies like I, Tonya, Ghostbusters: Afterlife, Annabelle Comes Homes and The Bad Seed. Mckenna has also acted on TV shows like The Haunting of Hill House and The Handmaid's Tale (receiving an Emmy nod for the latter).

While the late Philip Seymour Hoffman played Plutarch Heavensbee in The Hunger Games: Catching Fire as well as in parts one and two of Mockingjay, Jesse Plemons is taking on the role of the future Head Gamemaker and rebellion leader for this movie.And the actor isn't playing games when it comes to his performances. Throughout his career, Jesse has earned an Oscar nomination for his role in The Power of the Dog as well as Emmy nods for his parts in Love & Death, Black Mirror and Fargo, where he met his longtime love Kirsten Dunst.His other credits include Killers of the Flower Moon, The Irishman, Battleship and Breaking Bad.

Kelvin Harrison Jr. is taking on the part of Beetee, who's not only the winner of the 34th Hunger Games but also the father of 50th Games tribute Ampert Latier. In previous Hunger Games movies, Jeffrey Wright performed the role.While fans have certainly seen Kelvin in movies and TV shows—such as Genius, Chevalier, Waves, Luce and It Comes at Night to name a few—they've also heard his voiceover work in animated films like Mufasa: The Lion King.

Once you hear Maya Hawke is playing Wiress (a former Hunger Games winner, now District 12 mentor, played by Amanda Plummer in Catching Fire), you might get so excited you'll feel like your world is turned upside down.The actress—who's following in the famous footsteps of her parents Uma Thurman and Ethan Hawke—has previously played Jo March in the TV adaptation of Little Women, Eleanor in Do Revenge, Anxiety in Inside Out 2 and, of course, Robin in Stranger Things.

Originally played by the late Lynn Cohen in Catching Fire, the part of former-Hunger-Games-victor-turned-District-12-mentor Mags is now being portrayed by Lili Taylor.An Emmy nominee for her roles in American Crime and Six Feet Under, the actress has also appeared in The Conjuring, Mystic Pizza, Say Anything and I Shot Andy Warhol to name a few credits on a long list.

Also among the District 12 tributes is Wyatt Callow, who is portrayed by Ben Wang.In addition to being cast in the newest Hunger Games film, the actor has appeared in Karate Kid: Legends, the movie musical version of Mean Girls, Good Egg, Sight and American Born Chinese.

Ralph Fiennes is ruling over Panem as its dictator President Snow, a role previously played by Tom Blyth in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes and the late Donald Sutherland in Catching Fire and both parts of Mockingjay.The actor is a three-time Oscar nominee—being recognized for his roles in Conclave, The English Patient and Schindler's List—and a seven-time BAFTA contender, also receiving praise for his work in The Grand Budapest Hotel, Coriolanus, The Constant Gardener and The End Of The Affair. Plus, Ralph was up for an Emmy for his role in Bernard And Doris.

Molly McCann plays Louella, another District 12 tribute.The actress has already built up quite the résumé, appearing in TV shows like Bad Sisters, The Hardacres, The Boy That Never Was and Star Wars: Visions. As for her film credits, they include Herself, Freelance, Never Grow Old and Feed.

Portraying Louella's lookalike Lou Lou is Iona Bell, who's previously appeared in movies like Fing!, Savage Flowers and Frayed and TV shows like Mandrake.

Elle Fanning Takes on Role of Effie Trinket

The answer to who is playing Effie Trinket isn't completely unknown.While Elizabeth Banks performed the part in previous Hunger Game movies, Elle Fanning is now stepping into the shoes of this character (who, in Sunrise on the Reaping, is a stylist for Haymitch Abernathy ahead of the 50th Games).First appearing on screen alongside sister Dakota Fanning in 2001's I Am Sam, the actress has gone on to star in several more movies, including Maleficent, Somewhere, Super 8, The Beguiled and A Complete Unknown.On the TV side, Elle has acted in The Girl from Plainville as well as in The Great (earning an Emmy nomination for the latter).

While Stanley Tucci portrayed Hunger Games host Caesar Flickerman in the previous films, the franchise has found his successor for the role in Kieran Culkin. After making his acting debut as a kid in brother Macaulay Culkin's Home Alone, the actor went on to appear in movies like Father of the Bride, She's All That and Igby Goes Down. And while Kieran took a break from the craft, he came back to star in movies and TV shows like Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, Infinity Baby, Succession and A Real Pain, which landed him his first Oscar.,

Glenn Close is taking on the mean-spirited energy of District 12 tributes’ escort Drusilla Sickle.

Producer Nina Jacobs described Glenn as “a dream Drusilla” in a June 16 press release, adding, “She brings so much of her intellect and imagination to each role, creating characters who are unforgettable and iconic.”

Prior to her recent casting, the actress has stunned in films like Fatal Attraction, The Wife, Guardians of the Galaxy and Hillbilly Elegy.

Billy Porter slithered into the role of Magno Stift—Drusilla’s estranged husband and the District 12 tributes’ fashion designer—who often found inspiration for his looks in live reptiles.

It was Billy’s award-winning role in Pose that struck Nina. (He earned Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series for his role as Pray Tell in 2019.)

“Billy is one of those rare performers who can dazzle and devastate in equal measure on stage and screen,” she shared in a June 16 press release. “He made an indelible impression on me when we worked together on Pose, both as an actor and a human being.”

He has also starred in a number of projects, including American Horror Story, Cinderella and The Broken Hearts Club: A Romantic Comedy.

Francis Lawrence Is Directing The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Francis Lawrence has his playbook all set, having previously directed The Hunger Games: Catching Fire and Mockingjay parts one and two.Outside the franchise, he's helmed movies like Slumberland, See and Jennifer Lawrence's Red Sparrow as well as directed music videos for artists like Beyoncé's "Run the World (Girls)," Lady Gaga's "Bad Romance," Britney Spears' "Circus" and Jennifer Lopez's "Jenny From the Block."

Billy Ray Is the Screenwriter for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

Billy Ray is also a familiar face to the franchise, having adapted the OG film from Suzanne Collins' novel. His other work includes Terminator: Dark Fate, Flightplan and Captain Phillips, for which he received an Oscar nomination. In addition, Nina Jacobson and Brad Simpson are producing Sunrise on the Reaping and Cameron MacConomy is serving as executive producer.

#804. Clough's longevity: landmark achievement or indictment on football?

Nigel Clough took charge of Mansfield Town in November 2020

Becoming the longest-serving manager at a club takes some doing in the fickle world of football.

Sticking around at two clubs long enough to hold that mantle is just about unprecedented.

But Mansfield Town's Nigel Clough is about to redefine longevity as a manager when it comes to working at sides that make up the top 92 in the English pyramid.

"I don't think it's particularly an achievement; I think it's more an indictment of football that nobody else has lasted that long," Clough told BBC Sport.

This weekend he becomes the longest-serving manager â in terms of active years in the job and league matches at the helm â of the Stags, where he surpasses club great Ian Greaves.

The 16 years Clough spent at Burton Albion, which took in around 900 matches across two spells spanning more than two decades, means the record at the east Staffordshire side is already his.

Former England forward Clough is now six years and one week into the Stags job and is the second longest-serving manager across England's top four leagues - behind only Mikel Arteta at Arsenal - but he does not see his staying power as anything special.

"I don't really think about it that much, I have to say. I'm just trying to get through the week," said Clough, who has been in charge of Mansfield for 329 matches across all competitions.

While Clough's players, as well as Mansfield fans have a different take on what his lengthy tenure at the One Call Stadium has meant, the 60-year-old reeled off the names of legendary past managers - his late father and iconic Nottingham Forest boss Brian Clough included - when reflecting on what joy clubs would have by sticking by their manager.

"When you look back 20 or 30 years, my dad was at Forest for 18 years, Alex Ferguson was at Manchester United for so long and then there was Arsene Wenger at Arsenal. That was at the top level, but even lower down there was a lot of managers who stayed a lot of years," he said

"I just think it's sad the way football is going at the moment. The first bad period that people have, a month, two months or something like that, and the manager is the one that goes."

Clough, who played in the top flight for Forest, Liverpool and Manchester City, has been in management for 28 years and been in charge of just four clubs - Mansfield, Burton, Derby County and Sheffield United - in that time.

Since bounding from non-league level - where he spent the first 10 years of his management career in his first spell at Burton - to take the reins of Derby in the Championship in 2009, no-one has overseen more matches than Clough's 893 across England's top four divisions.

The latest statistics from the League Managers' Association show that managers across those leagues are now staying in their jobs for less than a year on average.

Clough bucking the trend with his record-setting endurance at Mansfield comes in the same week that Manchester United sacked Michael Carrick, when he was 10 months into the job, and Crystal Palace relieved Pierre Sage of his role after only 16 games.

When asked if Clough has ever felt his job was under threat during any "sticky period" at Mansfield, he responded with a firm "of course".

It was when the Stags were in the relegation places and on a 12-match winless run in his first full campaign in charge in 2021-22.

He survived that, then oversaw a club-record 11 consecutive home wins and went on to guide Mansfield to the League Two play-off final at Wembley later the same season.

"You've got to go through that period and you've got to get through it," Clough said of dealing with difficult runs as a manager.

"And I think as you get a little bit older, you know more that it's going to change.

"You get a result out of adversity as much as anything. If you're winning, it doesn't keep going, and if you're losing it's the same thing if you've got a reasonable team and you're doing the right things."

Clough: 'Six years have gone extremely quickly'

Mansfield boss Clough on 25 years 'in family business'

Nigel Clough's Mansfield side are 11th in the League One table after 13 games this season

While Mansfield missed out on promotion when they took their bid all the way to the national stadium in 2022, they went up automatically two years later when they finished third in the table.

It ended Mansfield's 21-year absence from the third tier. And when he kept them up in their first season back, Clough did what no-one had done for 35 years.

Last season they finished 10th, the club's highest league placing since 1987 when Greaves guided them to exactly the same position in the standings.

Stags supporter Dean Foulkes says it "has been an incredible journey" at Mansfield since Clough took the helm in November 2020.

At Burton he is a club legend for the way he transformed the Brewers as a non-league side in his first spell there before taking them to the Championship during his second stint.

He leapt a number of divisions when he left Burton the first time to manage Derby - a particularly poignant job as his father took the Rams to their first English title in 1972.

Even at Sheffield United, where Clough had the shortest stint of his managerial career, he guided them to the semi-final of the FA Cup when they were a League One side in 2014.

"He is really good football man to have around. We should be proud that he is Mansfield Town manager," Foulkes told BBC Radio Nottingham.

"Look at what he has achieved, promotion, and we now have players coming to Mansfield Town because they want to play for Nigel Clough."

It is why prolific veteran forward David McGoldrick moved there in the summer, and how the club has enticed former Leeds United forward Tyler Roberts, as well as ex-Preston forward Michael Smith to the Nottinghamshire town while also landing highly-rated Tottenham midfielder George Abbott on loan.

Ryan Sweeney says the chance to play for Clough was "the main reason" he decided to return to the club last summer.

Former Nottingham Forest and Southend striker Stephen McLaughlin says Clough "manages differently to any other manager" he has worked with.

"He doesn't treat you as a number, he treats you as a person and you want to run though bricks walls for him," McLaughlin said.

"It's hard to explain what he does for you on and off the pitch as well. You are not on the grass too long in training because he trusts you to get your work in and to be ready for Saturday.

"He doesn't give too much tactical information to people because the message is 'just do your job and work hard'."

Jordan Bowery has been asked to do that more than most, having been transformed from a striker to a defender and is now seen as 'Mr Versatile'., external

"He is incredibly loyal and trusts me in those positions," Bowery said. "A lot of managers wouldn't do that, but he's had my back and I appreciate that.

"He can get onto you, but that is like most managers. He expects and demands the best out of every single one of you each day.

"He has obviously been around the game a long time, played at the highest level - he knows the game and he knows the players."

A young Nigel Clough (right) pictured in 1978, sat alongside his father Brian in the Nottingham Forest dugout

And Clough, the player, is a former attacker of considerable repute in Nottinghamshire.

No-one has scored more than Clough's 131 goals for Forest over the past 113 years.

It was there, at Mansfield's high-profile county neighbours, where he thrived under his father who famously guided the Reds to the First Division title in 1978 before collecting back-to-back European Cups.

The manager that Clough is has been shaped by the successes he watched up close as a child and those he later revelled in as a player.

"When you're brought up in the household that we were brought up in and the environment we were brought up in, then we have a certain insight into what it takes to have a chance of being successful and what you expect of the team and everything," he said.

"And the empathy, I don't think you should ever forget that if you've been a player as well, how that feels when you have a rough time and so on."

And it is those players, and how they are found before investing in them that is the closest thing to revealing the secret to Clough's longevity.

"We don't like wasting the owners' money," he said.

"Whether it was at Burton when we were in the Dr Martens South [non-league level] or whether it's here at Mansfield Town, we try and look after it as best we can. And we have a responsibility to do that.

"We do as much in-depth research as we can on players. Character is the main feature of what we look at. We can see all the stuff on the videos of what they can do, then we watch them live and everything, but you have to delve really into the character and get a lot of references from players, coaches, managers.

"We take that very seriously. Each season we set out to just try and get a few better players in the squad.

"It's keeping the ball rolling, keeping the owners happy, keeping the supporters happy."

Additional reporting by BBC Radio Nottingham's David Jackson and Jake Garner.

#803. Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore

With comets out of the picture, attention now turns to asteroids or even Earth itself as the source of prebiotic chemistry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet.

Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth.

Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement.

Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets.For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely.

Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves.

In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS.

The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second).Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."

It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet.

However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth.

Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA.

However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars, because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity."This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet."

More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1, where all the planets are bunched up close.

In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive.

The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#802. How a reunion with scout Bompastor solved Chelsea's striker issue

Sonia Bompastor was working as Lyon's head of youth development when Melvine Malard played at Clairfontaine

Thousands of miles from home, a 14-year-old had an encounter that would change her life.

Nestled in a forest about an hour from Paris is France's national football academy at Clairefontaine. Famous for developing global stars such as Kylian Mbappe and Thierry Henry, it is also where a teenage Melvine Malard first met Sonia Bompastor in 2014.

Malard had travelled from Reunion Island, a French overseas territory in the Indian Ocean, to play in a football tournament. Watching from the sidelines was a titan of French football.

Bompastor, a two-time Champions League winner who had become Lyon's head of youth development, spotted the young forward and persuaded her to move to mainland France.

Twelve years later, the pair have been reunited at Chelsea. After joining from Manchester United in July, Malard has already established herself as a key player.

It took just six appearances for the 26-year-old to match her six-goal tally from last season's Women's Super League, helping fill the void left by Sam Kerr's departure.

"I knew she had the potential to be a really good player," Bompastor tells BBC Sport. "Having known her for so long and all the hard work she has put in, I'm really proud of her."

Convincing Malard's mother to let her daughter move nearly 6,000 miles from home was not straightforward - but Bompastor had a plan for the phone call.

"It's a lot of responsibility for you as a coach to bring a young player like this and move her from her own family," Bompastor says.

"The main thing for her mum in that phone call was she knew she could trust me as a manager but also as a woman."

For teenager Malard, the transition was difficult. She was close to her family and struggled with the bitterly cold winters of Lyon.

Because of its tropical climate, temperatures on Reunion Island rarely drop below 20C even in winter, whereas in Lyon, the mercury remains in low single figures during December and January.

Bompastor still laughs about one particular conversation with the young forward.

"She said to me: 'I'm so sorry, Sonia, but I think I need to go back to my place. It's so cold here. I can't play football any more!'" says Bompastor.

But Malard stuck around, knowing the opportunity was too good to turn down.

"When Lyon calls you, it's maybe just one time in your life," she says. "So you need to take your opportunity when it comes."

Bompastor's influence extended beyond football. As head of Lyon's academy, she also kept a close eye on Malard's education.

"When I did bad in school, she called me," Malard says. "'Mel, where are you? The school called me - it's not good what you're doing!'

"That was a nightmare - Sonia is always here."

Their relationship continued as Malard progressed through the ranks and finally broke into Lyon's first team as a 17-year-old in 2017.

By the time Bompastor had become the club's head coach for the 2021-22 season, Malard had established herself in the team and at the end of that campaign, she started the Champions League final against Barcelona as Bompastor's side secured a 3-1 victory.

For the boss, it remains a particularly special memory.

"When you look at all the journey and Melvine coming as a young kid into a different environment, far away from her family... and how she improved to be starting that game and for us to win that game," Bompastor says. "It's a big achievement."

Title race hots up before Chelsea-Man City showdown

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

Chelsea have had 13 different goalscorers in the WSL this season with Malard's six topping the list

Now reunited with her former boss at Chelsea, Malard has relished the responsibility of leading the line following Kerr's departure.

It took her just 341 minutes to chalk up six league goals for her new club. Last season, despite scoring four in the first two games, it was 17 matches and 1,206 minutes before she hit the same number for Manchester United.

Goals have come alongside frequently getting into dangerous positions.

At United in 2025-26, she averaged 3.4 shots and 6.2 touches in the opposition penalty area per 90 minutes. Those figures have risen to 5.4 and 11.8 respectively at Chelsea.

The quality of her opportunities has also improved. Her expected goals per 90 minutes have more than doubled from 0.5 to 1.1, while her shot conversion rate has increased from 10.5% to 22.2%.

It suggests Malard is benefiting from more opportunities in dangerous areas, while also making better use of the chances that come her way.

Bompastor believes the forward's improvement has been about more than just her goalscoring ability.

"She developed herself in terms of technical skills, knowledge of the game, understanding the game a little bit more, reading the game better," she says.

"She can play in different positions so we know we can use her as a nine or as a winger."

Such versatility has made Malard a valuable option for Bompastor as she chases silverware at home and abroad.

After winning the domestic treble during her first season in 2024-25, Chelsea only picked up the League Cup last season, with their third-placed finish snapping a run of six straight WSL titles.

Nine games into 2026-27, the Blues have the league's best attack and meanest defence, but a disappointing draw at home to Everton last weekend allowed champions Manchester City to overhaul them at the top of the table.

The two sides meet at Stamford Bridge on Saturday in a match live on BBC One that could be instrumental in deciding the title.

Malard will likely be leading the line, but Bompastor's ambitions for her former academy prospect are not limited to club level.

When Malard asks what Bompastor hopes she will achieve this season, the Chelsea boss sets her a clear challenge.

"I would like you to play for France next summer as the number nine and to win the World Cup," she says.

Twelve years after their first encounter, Bompastor continues to push Malard to new heights.

#800. Justin Bieber Pops Out at Rising British Star’s $30 Concert in L.A. in Surprise Cameo: ‘Who’s Gonna Pinch Me Then?’

The pop star jumped in on Finn Askew's song "Music All Over Her Body."

A couple of hundred people went into Finn Askew’s show in Los Angeles expecting to see the rising British singer, not one of the biggest pop stars in the world. But at The Moroccan Lounge on Thursday (Nov. 12), fans got both, with Justin Bieber popping out for a surprise cameo and duet.

As captured in footage posted by Askew on Instagram, Bieber took the stage at the end of the setlist, adding his signature runs and instantly recognizable voice to “Music All Over Her Body,” a single released by the Wellington, U.K., native in September. Under flashing lights and in front of a disbelieving crowd, Bieber — sporting slim sunglasses and a snazzy button-up shirt — trades lines of the song back and forth with Askew while grooving and swaggering to the music.

Billboard has reached out to Bieber’s rep for more details.

According to the venue’s website, its event capacity is about 250 people. “POV: Justin Bieber randomly performs at a $30 show,” one person wrote over a video of the duet taken from the audience’s perspective.

Bieber’s stop at the unusually small (by his standards) performance space comes just three days after he posed with an arm around the 25-year-old up-and-comer in a photo posted on Instagram. Askew simply captioned it, “Brother.”

Later, on his Story, Askew reflected on the experience. “who’s gonna pinch me then?” he wrote, later following up with: “I just got into bed and it’s all just hit me. tears of joy.”

The Brit has been making music since he was a teenager, creating debut single “Roses” when he was 16. He started properly releasing music in 2020 and unveiled EP Blueboy this past April.

Bieber hasn’t dropped music since his Billboard 200 No. 2 Swag double album, and he’s kept a lower profile since headlining Coachella this spring. He does seem to be developing a knack for spontaneous surprise performances, having showed up for an impromptu jam session in MacArthur Park in L.A. in September.

How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy, astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere.

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much. At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth. This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed.

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Alix is an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham specialising in the characterisation of stars and exoplanets. She is passionate about science communication, and how astrophysics is portrayed in movies, TV, and pop culture at large.

#797. Six goals to go - will McGinn catch Dalglish & Law?

As Scotland legend Kenny Dalglish watched one of his records equalled in Scotland's 2-1 win over North Macedonia, another of his feats loomed into view.

The night was supposed to be about Andy Robertson joining Dalglish as Scotland's most-capped man, the Tottenham left-back making his 102nd appearance for his country.

But instead, for the first time, the 75-year-old might be nervous that his crown as one of Scotland men's all-time top goalscorers is wobbling.

That is because, in Scotland's rather humdrum Nations League victory, John McGinn - in his 94th Scotland appearance - took two big strides towards the record.

The Aston Villa midfielder now has 24 goals for his country - six shy of Dalglish's long-standing record of 30, shared with Denis Law.

"It's something that's been in the back of my head," McGinn admitted in the post-match debrief. "If I start climbing that table, it means we've been successful as a team."

Now 32 years old, time is running out for him. But as he pulls level with Hughie Gallacher, one of the Wembley Wizards of folklore, his ambition is clear.

McGinn double gives drab Scotland win over North Macedonia

There was a time when talk of this record being toppled seemed laughable. Scotland has produced strikers in recent decades, but none close to Dalglish or Law.

The fact a midfielder might take the title makes McGinn's feat all the more astonishing.

His prowess in front of goal is no secret to the Tartan Army. There was the spell at the end of 2019 where he scored six in three games, his overhead kick against Austria, his late winner against Croatia in 2024.

But of late, his lack of goals and even his performances have had some fans questioning where he fits into the Scotland team.

"It has been a bit of a dry patch for me over the last year on the goal front," McGinn admitted, and he's not wrong.

He failed to find the back of the net for Scotland in 2025, the first time he'd done that since 2020.

But, just as his form at Villa has sky-rocketed, he came up big for his new international head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.

"Isn't it great to have a John McGinn in your team?" former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on Sportsound. "He's somebody you'd want to have in your team to be taking a penalty for you.

"I'd be surprised if John McGinn doesn't get the goal record now. It might take him another year or two, but he is definitely capable of getting that record."

Becoming Scotland's main penalty taker will help, a fact McGinn alluded to coyly post-match.

In his career, he had only taken one spot-kick before this season - scoring for Scotland in the 3-3 draw against Norway back in 2023.

In this campaign he has scored three and missed one, smacking the bar against Fulham on Halloween.

In classic McGinn fashion, he bounced back to slot home against Manchester United the following week, before being caught on ref-cam admitting to the official that he was nervous to take it after his hitting the woodwork.

That jovial, lovable personality has not just won him fans off the pitch. It is clear that his team-mates at both Villa and the national team adore him.

"He's not going to stop until he [gets the record]," said striker Che Adams, who helped set up McGinn's first against North Macedonia.

"Everyone's pleased for him, he's the best person I've met in football. For him to get the recognition he deserves is amazing."

McGinn's iconic status in Scottish football is secure and will not be tarnished if he fails to climb the mountain.

Whether it is being speared by Steven Thompson in training, calling Scotland performances 'jobby', or admitting he would "probably be at Yeovil" were it not for his backside, the midfielder has already won the heart of a nation.

#796. The Rainmaker Kills Off Character With Gruesome Beheading

The Rainmaker season two just killed off a major character, their head found in Bruiser’s designer handbag. Here are all the gory details.

This Rainmaker death will make fans lose their heads.

And in this case, that expression takes on a fairly literal meaning. While it seemed like Tom Cassady (Austin Nichols) had his death sentence written at the close of episode four, he wasn’t the victim of the Nov. 13 episode.

Instead, it was Miss Doppler Dumbass herself. Lynette, Tom’s new wife played by Sarah O’Connor, found her head separated from her body and stuffed into the designer handbag now in the possession of Bruiser (Lana Parrilla).

The beginnings of Lynette’s dark fate were teased in episode four, when it was revealed that Tom’s gambling debts hadn’t actually gotten him—as well as the attorneys of J. Lyman Stone—mixed up with the likes of Gator Jack Guidry (Owen Roe).

Instead, the former pro baseball player was covering for his wife’s own money loss. After all, the weatherwoman was looking for other lucrative avenues when Tom’s pro career (and the buckets of money she thought would come with it) was cut short.

Once Bruiser made the connection, however, she stressed that Lynette and Tom must remain married to ensure they don’t have to test against one another.

So, a drunk Lynette—devastated that she is further chained to her disappointing marriage—rushed to the headquarters of Gator’s operations, begging the crime boss to help her out of her situation.

But while it seemed like he’d take out Tom, Gator felt Lynette to be the looser of the two ends and cut her life short. As for exactly how, where, when and who? That’s all still left to be determined.

For Austin, making the bloody discovery was intimidating.

“There's a funny story behind this,” the actor, who joined season two of the hit show, told USA Network. “We have so many light, fun scenes. And then I remember getting a call sheet and it saying, ‘Tomorrow, you're going to discover your wife's head in a purse.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, okay, I got to act. I got to be serious. I got to do some real work here.’”

As he put it, finding a head in a handbag is “not something you see every day. It's super high stakes.”

#795. Who Is Sara Schell, The Newcomer Who Won Songwriter of the Year at the 2026 Latin Grammys?

Meet the Venezuelan behind hits by KATSEYE, Becky G, J Balvin & other major stars.

EDITOR’S NOTE: This story has been updated with Schell’s victory.

In 2020, Sara Schell was planning to move to London to study business after graduating high school in Venezuela. On Thursday (Nov. 12), she won the Latin Grammy Award for songwriter of the year, and was also nominated for best pop song as a co-writer of Kany García’s “A La Niña Que Fui.”

At 23, Schell was not the only woman in the songwriter of the year category, but she was the only newcomer. She appeared alongside veterans like Edgar Barrera (who boasted 82 Latin Grammy nominations and 29 wins, including songwriter of the year for the past three years), Yoel Henríquez (who had garnered 23 nominations and three victories), Iván Gámez and Jenni Mosello (with a total of four nominations each).

Her credits listed by the Latin Recording Academy included “A La Niña Que Fui” by García, “Ahí Estabas Tú” and “Barco de Papel” by Fonseca, “Bendito” by Rawayana, “Si Te Vas” by J Balvin and Jay Wheeler (which reached No. 1 on Billboard‘s Latin Airplay chart), and “Vas a Quedarte” by Diego Torres and Manuel Carrasco. She’s also been behind chart hits like “Gabriela” by KATSEYE (No. 21 on the Hot 100), “Mercedes” by Becky G and Óscar Maydon (No. 1 on Regional Mexican Airplay) and “Ojos verdes” by Nicki Nicole (No. 1 on the Billboard Argentina Hot 100).

But how did this young woman from Barquisimeto go from wanting to study business to writing for major stars?

“In 2020, I graduated high school and then the pandemic hit, so we decided to move to Mexico. When we arrived, I was supposed to go to London to study business because I had always said I wanted a career, but at that moment, all the universities were shut down, so we had to do what everyone else did: stay home and find something to do,” Schell tells Billboard Español in an interview from Spain during a break from a songwriting session. “I started posting covers and other things on Instagram, and that’s how I connected with several writers online, started doing Zoom sessions and writing together.”

Schell’s musical training began at the age of four at the Vicente Emilio Sojo Conservatory, a prestigious institution founded in 1936 in Barquisimeto, Lara State, which works closely with Venezuela’s National System of Youth and Children’s Orchestras and Choirs, a.k.a. El Sistema. There, she played the cello until she was 14 — a “super magical experience” that allowed her to travel to Peru and the U.S. representing her country. She also took piano and singing lessons.

At 15, she wrote her first song, “Sin Ti o Contigo,” which she uploaded to digital platforms, though it has since been taken down. “I remember I was falling asleep and a melody came to me, so I got up and went to the bathroom so I wouldn’t wake anyone up. What inspired me was that I was dating this guy, and we had broken up, so I started pouring it all out,” she says. “Then my heart was broken, and that’s when you start writing — because, you know, everyone needs therapy.”

But Schell didn’t know people in her circle who could actually make a living from music, so she considered a more conventional university education necessary to “move forward.”

It was her father who advised her not to leave and to try her luck in music — “‘Try what you’ve always loved,’ he told me, ‘give it two years'” — because his own parents hadn’t encouraged him to pursue his dreams. “My dad played music, did sports, he was great at everything, and my grandfather would say: ‘No, you’re going to study this.’ So with me, he did the complete opposite.”

Her first break came in 2024 with Fuerza Regida after a brief trip to Miami, where she went with a demo of her songs and the idea of finding someone in the industry she’d heard about but “only knew his name was Ben,” Schell says. There, she managed to have two or three songwriting sessions a day with different colleagues, and her name reached the ears of Nir Seroussi of Interscope, who contacted her to learn more about her work. “At that moment, I didn’t know who Nir was. I told him: ‘Yeah, sure, let’s meet.’ But I had no idea what I was walking into.”

Upon meeting Seroussi, Schell says he immediately made her feel “like family,” and after listening to a couple of her songs, introduced her to Ben Tischker of Wide Eyed Entertainment — the very same “Ben” she had originally been looking for — who is now her manager. “It was incredible!” Schell says. “Then Nir helped me place a couple of songs, including my first one, ‘PXTXS,’ for Fuerza Regida.

Originally written as a bolero, “PXTXS” — part of Fuerza’s album Dolido Pero No Arrepentido — is a heartbreak song about trying to overcome a breakup through excess and self-destruction. “It was a song that got a lot of attention at the time because it was a bolero that wasn’t vulgar but very raw,” says Schell. “I remember they replicated what I was doing with my voice on a guitar, and then they made it more regional. It turned out very beautiful.”

Through Interscope, the hit “Gabriela” by KATSEYE also came about. “It was quite strange because it happened very fast. They needed me to write a bridge in Spanish, and I remember sending Nir two options. He said, ‘This one,’ sent it, and that was it,” she recalls. “Normally songs take much longer to come out, but two months later the song was released and I started receiving tons of messages: ‘Congrats, congrats.’ I didn’t even know KATSEYE was such a big group. And well, obviously it came out, and with everything that happened with the song, I’m very grateful to be part of it.”

Since then, she mentions Rawayana’s “Bendito” (“It was super fun to write, a blast”) and Kany García’s “A La Niña Que Fui” (“It was very beautiful how we connected”) among her favorite collaborations.

In her August cover story interview with Billboard Español, García praised Schell as a “super-talented” songwriter while recounting how this song, now competing for a Latin Grammy, came to be. (Its songwriting credits also include Rafa Arcaute, Nate Campany and Richi López).

“I called her to write. I had melodies in my head, but nothing concrete… And she said to me — because it wasn’t me, it was her: ‘Hey, how about writing a song to your inner child?'” García recalled. “It gave me chills, because she didn’t know that the project was heading in that direction. And I told myself: ‘How beautiful it is that sometimes, as a songwriter, I think I have to do it all myself, that everything has to come from my head. But when you sit with creative people who are seeing the picture from outside, they see things that you don’t.”

“Just meeting her, and how I grasped what she wanted without her telling me,” says Schell, “sometimes there’s this energy in the room that’s the most important, where the most magical songs come from, and I feel like we walked in and captured it right away.”

Although she has released some music as a singer in the past year — mostly collaborations with Sistek, Gonza Silva and LAGOS — Schell, currently signed to MPub and Wide Eyed Publishing, says her “calling” has always been “writing for others” and that she doesn’t plan to have a career as a performer.

“From the moment we met Sara, we recognized an exceptional talent in her,” Daniela Méndez Varón, head of A&R at MPub, tells Billboard. “Her artistic sensitivity, versatility and vision as a songwriter set her apart, but it’s her human qualities that make her even more special.”

As for how she found out about her Latin Grammy nominations, the songwriter recalls going to bed exhausted after a long day’s work and not even setting her alarm to catch the announcement. “But obviously, I was nervous,” she says. “I left my phone’s sound on, and I got a call from producer Héctor Mazzarri, who’s one of my best friends — also nominated this year, by the way — telling me: ‘Congratulations.’ And I’m like: ‘What happened?’ ‘Songwriter of the Year.’ I was like: ‘Oh my God.'”

Meanwhile, her dad couldn’t be prouder: “He’s so happy. I mean, of course he could believe it. So he’s like: ‘I knew it from the beginning.’ It’s very sweet.”

When asked who she’d like to write songs with, Schell doesn’t hesitate. “Franco De Vita. You know, being from Venezuela, I grew up listening to him, and it was the music I listened to most with my grandparents,” she says with a smile.

#794. Tuchel to remind England of anti-racism protocols before Spain game

England are three points behind Spain at the top of their Nations League group

Manager Thomas Tuchel will remind England's players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols before Sunday's Nations League fixture against Spain in Madrid.

The match will be England's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious fixture at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.

The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt.

"We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place.

"Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."

European governing body Uefa, the organiser of the Nations League, has a three-step protocol to handle incidents of discrimination inside stadiums, designed to give referees the power to halt matches, and even abandon games if racist behaviour continues.

In the first instance, referees halt the match and request an announcement on the public address system.

Then, if discrimination continues, officials can stop the game for five to 10 minutes and take the players from the field.

If issues continue after the second stoppage, then the game can be abandoned.

"It's important that the players know about the protocol," Tuchel said.

"And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."

Who would make your England-Spain combined XI?

England's black players such as Ashley Cole and Rio Ferdinand were subject to racist chanting during the 2004 friendly in Madrid

Sunday's fixture takes place at Atletico Madrid's home, the Metropolitano.

Victory would ensure England win their Nations League group and earn a more favourable quarter-final draw but world champions Spain are unbeaten in 43 matches, including a 3-2 win at Wembley in September.

"It's important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength," Tuchel added.

"It [Spain] is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost.

"I think we're there, and I think we're ready to win on Sunday,"

#793. Young Thug Responds to Quavo’s Attempt to Have Him Reconcile With Gunna: ‘How Uma Fix Some Sh– I Didn’t Break Qua?’

Offset detailed why he stood by Gunna following the YSL RICO trial during a Popcast appearance.

Once a hip-hop capital and the genre’s centrifugal force, Atlanta’s rap scene has seen a decline and become a fractured community since the sprawling YSL RICO trial.

Offset joined New York Times’ Popcast on Thursday (Nov. 12), during which he explained why he stood by Gunna after the “Fukumean” rapper faced allegations of snitching once he reached an Alford plea deal in the YSL RICO case in 2022 to regain his freedom.

The decision caused a rift with some of his previous close collaborators like Young Thug and Lil Baby, who haven’t worked with Gunna since.

“He ain’t told on nobody,” Offset stated. “We from the town. I done been through the cap internet storm of people wanting you to show that you’re down… I’m not a follower, I rock with who rock with me. I rock with who I rock with. If I fall off, I don’t want you to say, ‘F me.’ I done been through stuff and seen peers like, ‘I’ma get away.'”

He continued: “We partners. We friends… All that bull divided our city and it made each artist pay for it. The difference is Atlanta, we got unity… There was always things going on between the artists in Atlanta. There’s always politics. We always showed unity. I look at how I got on, Thug got on, everybody got on the same train. And it only worked because of the unity.”

Offset recruited Gunna to join him on his GMFU album cut “Spit Propane,” which arrived on Friday (Nov. 13). The Migos rapper wants to see Atlanta hip-hop’s scene unified once again like it was when the ATL trio rose to stardom in the mid-2010s.

“I just really wish we was all just unified because we ran the whole hip-hop scene. Now it’s a gap. It ain’t no real city running hip-hop, which makes hip-hop drain and lose its powers,” he added. “You killing your own product.”

Quavo got wind of Offset’s rant and posted to his Instagram Story on Thursday, calling for Thug to work things out and reconcile with his YSL mentee, Gunna, for the betterment of ATL.

“We all family @thuggerthugger1 we all some playas,” Quavo wrote. “We gon fix it or lets hit.”

However, Thugger quickly replied with an explanation that, from his view, he wasn’t the one who broke the relationship with Gunna.

“How Uma fix some shit I didn’t break qua?” Thugger wrote. “I been a real man since day one, no n—a on this earth can tell u I lead then wrong or f–ked them over.”

Young Thug and Gunna haven’t collaborated since Thug reached a plea deal in the YSL RICO case and was released in October 2024. Gunna hasn’t spoken out about where their relationship stands either, as it seems to be icy on both sides.

Thug made an appearance on Lil Baby’s Fresh album standout “All My Partnas,” which was released earlier in November. Baby has also distanced himself from Gunna since the case.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program and set the stage for the Apollo progam to land on the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin. NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program. Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11, and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13.

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview. "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station. As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon.

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#791. Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

Toby Alderweireld was part of the Tottenham team that reached the Champions League final under Mauricio Pochettino

Mauricio Pochettino heads to Old Trafford with a reputation for "brutal" pre-seasons, an obsession with fitness and a no-nonsense approach.

Manchester United confirmed on Friday that Pochettino will become their manager on 18 November - replacing Michael Carrick - and has signed a contract until June 2029.

So what should the players and staff expect when the Argentine takes control at the end of next week?

BBC Sport spoke to Toby Alderweireld, who spent four years playing for Pochettino at Tottenham during a successful period where they reached the Champions League final and finished second in the Premier League.

How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd

Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better

Alderweireld, 37, says Pochettino has a no-nonsense approach to management and that he can get the best out of a squad, as long as you do it his way.

"He is very approachable but you need to follow his plan. If you don't follow his plan, you go on the side and you're not coming back any more.

"You need to think about team, team, team. If you're thinking about yourself, you're gone.

"As a player you have your own life, your own situation but he says 'look, I understand and you can talk to me about it but the team is number one' - that's the way it is and if you're not following it, he'll put you on the sideline.

"He's straightforward, has his own ideas and maybe you agree with them or don't, that's up to you. But you need to follow him and I think that's something Manchester United need - a big character, everyone in the same direction, following the plan and if not, no problem, you can go. He's the main man.

"He's a very smart man, knows how to talk to the press and what to say. He will create an environment like 'it's us against the world' - we are getting fit, we are together as a team. It doesn't matter what people say, let's work together and get results together.

"At Spurs there was coaching staff but he will be there. He knows everything. If he's not there, he's looking at video and data. He knows everything about the players on and off the pitch - the players will be watched.

"He is, in a positive way, a control freak because he says your body is your weapon and it needs to be ready to perform."

Does Alderweireld think Pochettino is right for Man Utd?

Manchester United have been criticised this season for an apparent lack of fitness and for not running enough in games - they rank in the bottom five in the league for distance covered and most high-intensity runs.

Alderweireld says Pochettino's number one demand is fitness and running.

"First of all he made us very fit. Pre-season was brutal.

"The way he wants to play - on the front foot, putting people under pressure, a high line, very dynamic play - you need to run. You need to be capable of running and be capable of high intensity runs - the basic is to be fit.

"Every manager wants a good pre-season and time to give the players their ideas and the fitness. But the players are going to feel straight away that it's a different level.

"This is every day at the training ground, it's 100% - that's what he asks, what he demands. It will be a big difference for the players and they're going to see results there straight away.

"In the Champions League semi-final, we were 3-0 down [against Ajax] and he didn't have a tactical half-time talk. He just said 'you're going to be physical, you're going to fight, you only need one goal to be back in the game, believe that everything is possible'.

"That was a big moment because we were nowhere near Ajax at that time, especially in that game. But we changed everything by intensity, by duels. I remember the long ball to [Fernando] Llorente and just fighting and asking 'how badly do you want it?' It changed from that moment."

The free AT&T Playoff Playlist Live festival happens Jan. 23-24 in Las Vegas.

The 2027 College Football Playoff National Championship will see two top teams competing on Jan. 25 at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas. Before that, a heavy-hitting lineup of DJs will provide pump-up music before the big game. Explore Alison Wonderland David Guetta John Summit See latest videos, charts and news

This year’s edition of AT&T Playoff Playlist Live – The CFP Music Festival will happen Jan. 23-24 at Las Vegas’ Grand Prix Plaza, located just off the Strip. The night 1 lineup will feature David Guetta, Marshmello, Alison Wonderland, Honeyluv and Girl Math, the duo made up of Nala and VNNSA. On day 2, the lineup will feature John Summit, Fisher, Sofi Tukker, Korolova and DJ Skilah. Doors open at 3 p.m. both days.
