#789. In Canada: Canada Music Fund to Receive $67M Boost; Women in Music Executive Award Winners Share Their Wisdom

Also this week: Sean Paul appears on the first episode of Billboard Canada News.

The Canada Music Fund is getting a new boost from the federal government.

At last night’s ADISQ Gala in Montreal (Nov. 8), the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture, Marc Miller, announced that the federal government will invest $67 million to the Canada Music Fund, as part of the government’s promised $600 million investment into the cultural sector. The sum was first announced in June to provide “immediate relief” to the country’s audio and audiovisual sector and confirmed for 2026-27 in the latest federal budget, which was tabled last week. Over the weekend, Ottawa gave a long-awaited breakdown of how the funds will be allocated.

The music sector will receive its share of the relief investment through the Canada Music Fund, which was renewed through 2028 last year. The $67 million sum will be distributed to the five organizations that the fund supports, with FACTOR (Foundation Assisting Canadian Talent on Recordings) receiving $31.5 million, Musicaction (which funds and supports Francophone music and music companies) receiving $21 million, the Canadian Starmaker Fund receiving $5.7 million, the RadioStar fund receiving $3.8 million and the Indigenous Music Office (IMO) receiving $5 million.

Last November, the IMO released a new national report outlining ways in which the federal government could help Indigenous artists and their music connect with bigger audiences, notably through increased discoverability on streaming platforms. Each of the funds will help support and foster emerging Canadian acts and help them compete on the world stage.

“Canada’s cultural sovereignty depends on our willingness to invest in our own voices,” says Meg Symsyk, president and CEO of FACTOR. “We have extraordinary talent in this country. Our responsibility is to give that talent the opportunity to be heard, to build lasting careers and to reach audiences here at home and around the world. This investment in the Canada Music Fund backs Canadian artists and the independent businesses that help bring their music to life. We thank Prime Minister Carney, Minister Champagne, Minister Miller and the Government of Canada for recognizing that investing in Canadian music is an investment in who we are.”

FACTOR, along with the Indigenous Music Office, CIMA, ADISQ, Bell Media, Spotify and more all participated in CRTC public hearings last year to discuss how to support Canadian Content.

Now, FACTOR welcomes the government’s investment and highlights how it will support the Canadian music sector.

“Behind every dollar invested in Canadian music are artists taking the next step in their careers and Canadian companies helping them get there,” says Symsyk. “Sustained investment makes it possible to look beyond the next release or tour and build for the future.”

Several other music organizations across Canada are celebrating the news, with the Canadian Live Music Association (CLMA) saying it is “thrilled to see government recognize the value that music brings to Canada, its businesses, and its communities.” The Canadian Independent Music Association (CIMA) calls the additional funding an “important step toward strengthening the industrial ecosystem that supports the development of great Canadian artists.”

“For years, CIMA has argued that the best way to ensure Canadians hear Canadian voices is to build a strong ecosystem of dynamic, globally competitive Canadian music companies serving excellent Canadian artists,” says Andrew Cash, president and CEO of CIMA. “These are the businesses that discover, develop and nurture artists, produce and promote Canadian music, help build audiences and create opportunities for Canadian artists to reach listeners both at home and around the world. This investment is an important commitment, and a clear indication that the government has listened to the music sector.”

The federal government’s new investment intends to bring stability to the cultural sector as “longer-term policy, regulatory and market conditions evolve,” such as the Online Streaming Act, whose implementation continues to be the subject of much debate between the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC), streaming giants and the United States, which has made the CanCon fund requirements for major foreign-owned streaming services a sticking point in trade negotiations.

The live music sector is thriving more than ever in Canada. In her role as chief commercial officer of Live Nation Canada, Melissa Bubb-Clarke is helping it soar towards new heights.

On Nov. 24, she will accept the Executive of the Year Award at Billboard Canada Women In Music, recognizing the important work she does behind the scenes, helping Canada’s live music giant scale its operations amid a rapidly growing industry, through collaborating and partnering with corporate brands.

The market leader in the country, Live Nation Canada has seen record success and revenue figures over the last few years, but in many ways Bubb-Clarke and the team she works with are just laying the foundation for an even bigger future.

In its second season this summer, the 50,000-capacity Rogers Stadium welcomed a new record number of 20 concerts to Toronto, drawing record-setting tours by headliners like Bruno Mars, BTS, Karol G and more. RBC Amphitheatre also kicked off its first season under its new name and partnership with RBC, which arrived alongside plans to become a year-round venue by 2030. There are more A-list artists coming to town than ever, but beyond welcoming shows, Bubb-Clarke is vying to create venues that offer an optimal experience for not just the artists playing them, but also the fans coming to see their favourite artist.

Preparing to accept the Billboard Canada Executive of the Year Award has given Bubb-Clarke the opportunity to reflect on the major strides she and her team have been making in the live music landscape over the past several years.

In an interview with Billboard Canada, Bubb-Clarke compares music to her work in sports at her previous company Maple Leafs Sports & Entertainment (MLSE), which owns the Toronto Maple Leafs and Toronto Raptors.

“I can give you a million reasons why I think music is as much of a compelling offering, if not more, than sports. There are more concerts at Scotiabank Arena than there are [Maple] Leafs and Raptors games combined. From a demographic standpoint, we’re serving everything to everybody with our 4,000+ shows that we do across Canada here with Live Nation. We do every demographic, every age group, all sorts of styles of music, I think we are super fan-friendly in that way.”

“I think we have been able to understand what the fans have come to get, what they have been able to experience at a sports venue. They’re looking for a similar experience at a show. They want to be able to have nice food and go to a specific place post-show or pre-show and have a great overall experience.”

In her dual role as the president of MusiCounts and the chief operating officer of CARAS, the organization behind the Juno Awards and the Canadian Music Hall of Fame, Kristy Fletcher influences every stage of a Canadian musician’s career.

Through music education charity MusiCounts, she’s there at the beginning, providing access to instruments and musical education to give youth a chance to make music in the first place. At CARAS, she’s able to foster and develop the industry and recognize artists at the Juno Awards. That continues all the way until the later stages of their career, when they become Hall of Famers.

On Nov. 24, Fletcher will accept the Impact Award at Billboard Canada Women In Music, recognizing the important work she does affecting musicians both onstage and in classrooms, from Rush’s surprise comeback performance at the 2026 Juno Awards to young students who might be Canada’s next breakthrough rock stars.

This year, MusiCounts announced a $1.4 million donation to support music education in Canadian schools, the biggest investment in the company’s history. Through the MusiCounts School Music Funding Programs, 96 schools across the country will receive support for their music programs amid increasing budget cuts and deficits in Ontario and throughout Canada.

“Music is such a foundational and fundamental part of development and growth for kids,” Fletcher says. “Think of all of the incredible benefits that music has on kids. It’s a way to sort out their emotions or express their feelings and thoughts, and it can improve mental health among youth. We have seen so many studies [showing how] music supports strong and healthy mental health, and develops positive self-esteem. There are studies showing improved cognitive abilities with playing music.

“MusiCounts has to be there to help fill in some of those gaps, and the gaps do grow. We’ve been doing this work for almost 30 years and we’ve allocated over $22 million to schools and community programs across the country. You would think we would maybe be nearing the end of the work we have to do, and that’s just not the case. We’re just scratching the surface. But that has allowed us to increase our programming.”

Read the full interview here. — Richard Trapunski

“Canada has influenced my music in many ways,” says Sean Paul.

The Jamaican star is the subject of the first episode of Billboard Canada News, live now.

In a revealing half-hour interview hosted by Alicia West, Paul talks about the important role that Canada played in his come-up. He guested on the Baby Blue Sound Crew song “Money Jane” with Toronto hip-hop and R&B heroes Kardinal Offishall and Jully Black.

“I was just telling somebody last night. They asked me who was the first person to put you on, give you a collab? And I said Kardi. Kardi Offishall,” he says. “First person to pay me, first person to put me on a track, I always say.”

He also talks about shooting important breakthrough music videos “Gimme The Light” and “Get Busy” with Canadian director Director X (then Little X) and dancer/choreographer Tanisha Scott, both longtime collaborators. His connection goes back even further, with his grandfather living in Scarborough, Ontario when he was young.

It’s a wide-ranging conversation about his whole career, from his biggest chart hits to his collaborations with major pop stars like Rihanna and Sia. He also talks about his support of Jamaica following Hurricane Melissa.

Watch the full interview on Billboard Canada News below. — Richard Trapunski

Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound.

Fast radio bursts, or FRBs, are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star.

Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources.

As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now."Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them.

The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling.

The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website, the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old.

Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email.

Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old. The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur.

This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA.

Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email.

"The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement.

"It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#787. SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism

For nearly 90 years, physicists have divided magnetic materials into two main categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. Now, scientists have confirmed that a third type exists, revealing a previously unrecognized form of magnetic behavior that could lead to major advances in computing and electronics.

The breakthrough comes from a research team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. In a study published in Science, the researchers presented compelling experimental evidence for altermagnetism, a distinct magnetic phase that combines important characteristics of the two traditionally recognized types.

"In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy," explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. "Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase -- altermagnetism -- is real."

The team focused on manganese telluride (MnTe), a material that had long been classified as an antiferromagnet. Building on earlier research, the scientists identified direct evidence of chirality, a distinctive asymmetry in the material's magnetic structure. This property resembles the way a spiral staircase or screw twists in a particular direction and provides a crucial signature of altermagnetism.

Beyond its importance for fundamental physics, the finding could help researchers develop magnetic materials with properties suited to future technologies, including advanced memory systems, quantum devices, and more energy-efficient data centers.

Understanding the Two Traditional Types of Magnetism

Magnetism is familiar from everyday experiences, whether it is a refrigerator magnet holding up a photograph or a compass aligning with Earth's magnetic field. But the physics behind these effects is far more complicated than it appears.

At the atomic level, magnetism is connected to a quantum property of electrons known as spin. Although spin is not literally an electron rotating like a tiny ball, it behaves in certain ways as though the electron has its own angular momentum. Scientists commonly describe the two possible spin orientations as "up" and "down."

When these spins become organized into particular patterns, a material can exhibit magnetic properties. However, that does not necessarily mean it will produce an externally detectable magnetic field.

In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins align in the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down). Their combined effect produces the familiar magnetic field associated with ordinary magnets. People have used materials with this behavior for thousands of years.

A second category, identified in 1933, works differently. In antiferromagnets, neighboring electron spins point in opposite directions (up-down-up-down). Because the magnetic contributions oppose one another, they cancel out, leaving no overall magnetization.

A Third Type of Magnetism Challenges the Old Rules

For almost nine decades, these two categories provided the basic framework for understanding how magnetic order arises in materials. However, experimental observations in recent years began revealing behavior that neither category could fully explain.

Some materials displayed alternating electron spins and no overall magnetization, just like antiferromagnets. Yet they could also support useful spin currents, a property associated with ferromagnetic behavior. Spin currents allow information to be carried through the spin properties of electrons rather than relying entirely on their electrical charge.

The unusual combination suggested that scientists were dealing with something fundamentally different. In 2022, researchers introduced the term "altermagnets" for materials belonging to this proposed third magnetic class.

The key difference lies in the arrangement of atoms within the material. Altermagnets have alternating spin orientations (up-down-up-down), but the crystal structures surrounding the oppositely aligned spins are rotated relative to one another.

This rotation breaks a form of symmetry that exists in conventional antiferromagnets. Although the distinction is subtle, it can dramatically change how electrons behave, allowing altermagnets to combine properties once considered incompatible.

Scientists Find the Missing Evidence for Altermagnetism

Even as experimental support for altermagnetism accumulated, researchers still needed a decisive way to establish that it represented a genuinely distinct magnetic phase.

"By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real," Jost said, "but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle."

That missing evidence involved chirality, a property sometimes described as "handedness." An object is chiral when its mirror image cannot be perfectly aligned with the original. Human hands provide a simple example: Your left and right hands are mirror images, but a left hand cannot fit properly into a right-handed glove.

In an altermagnet, the unusual arrangement of atoms and electron spins can create this kind of handedness in the material's electronic and magnetic structure. Conventional antiferromagnets do not exhibit the same characteristic chiral signature.

Detecting that difference would provide a powerful way to distinguish a true altermagnet from a material that merely resembles one.

The researchers selected manganese telluride as their test material. For decades, scientists considered it an ordinary antiferromagnet, but more recent studies had raised the possibility that it belonged to the newly proposed category.

Powerful X-Rays Reveal a Hidden Magnetic Signature

To investigate the material's unusual properties, the team conducted experiments at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France. The facility's ID32 beamline produces precisely controlled polarized X-rays, allowing scientists to examine subtle magnetic structures that are otherwise extremely difficult to detect.

The researchers used circularly polarized X-rays, which have electric fields that rotate in either a left-handed or right-handed direction as the light travels. By measuring how the material scattered these two forms of light, they could search for evidence of chirality.

"Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams," explained Jost. "Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way."

The experiment revealed a clear difference in the way manganese telluride interacted with the two X-ray polarizations. This distinctive chiral response was precisely the kind of signal expected from altermagnetism and would not be present in a conventional antiferromagnet.

"This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own," Jost said.

The researchers first performed the experiment in 2024. They returned in early 2025 and repeated the measurements, successfully reproducing the results and strengthening the evidence for the new magnetic phase.

"This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties," said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. "Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible."

Why Altermagnetism Could Transform Future Computers

The discovery could have important consequences for spintronics, a growing field that seeks to use electron spin to develop more capable electronic devices.

Conventional electronics store and process information primarily by controlling the electrical charge of electrons. Spintronics adds another way to work with information by taking advantage of electron spin as well.

This extra capability could enable devices that operate faster, withstand interference more effectively, and consume substantially less electricity. Such improvements would be especially valuable in computer memory, large data centers, and other technologies that require enormous amounts of information processing.

However, the two traditional types of magnetism present different obstacles that have limited the development of spintronic systems.

"Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields," Jost explained. "If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible -- so you can't easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents."

Altermagnets offer a potentially valuable alternative. Like antiferromagnets, their opposing spins produce no overall magnetization, helping protect them against unwanted magnetic interference. At the same time, their unusual electronic structure allows them to generate spin-polarized currents that can be used to retrieve information.

"Altermagnets combine the best of both," Jost said. "They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with."

A New Frontier for Quantum Technology and Electronics

Confirming altermagnetism gives scientists a new class of materials to investigate and potentially engineer for technological applications. By combining magnetic stability with the ability to manipulate spin-based information, these materials could help overcome challenges that have held back conventional spintronic devices.

The next step will be learning how to control altermagnetic states using external influences such as light and electricity. Researchers hope that mastering this control will make it possible to design practical devices that take advantage of the unusual magnetic properties.

Although significant development is still needed before these materials can be widely used, the findings establish a stronger experimental foundation for future work on quantum technologies, computer memory, and more efficient data centers.

The research received partial funding from the DOE Office of Science.

Materials provided by SLAC. Original written by Erin Woodward. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#785. Producer Kevin J. Walsh Had Seen It All. Then ‘Being Heumann’ Came Along

The Oscar-nominated producer helped open doors for the disabled community on the set of Sian Heder's latest pic: "I'm as proud of what we did behind the scenes to redefine access as I am of the quality of this movie."

Being Heumann producer Kevin J. Walsh is not easily rattled.

After all, the Boston-area native served in a variety of assistant roles for Scott Rudin, Steven Spielberg and Tommy Mottola before eventually spending more than five years running Ridley Scott’s company, Scott Free. There, he shepherded a dozen pictures, four of them directed by Scott, including All the Money in the World (2017), The Last Duel (2021), House of Gucci (2021) and Napoleon (2023). In other words, he’s as battle-tested as they come.

Yet the prospect of helping CODA director Sian Heder tell the story of Judith “Judy” Heumann’s Herculean fight to make the world more accessible for disabled people made Walsh’s blood run cold. Related Stories Movies Sam Levy, Jamie Ramsay Offer Advice to Up-and-Coming Cinematographers: "What You Guys Do Lives Forever" Movies Ridley Scott Will Miss Academy's Governors Awards, Accept Honorary Oscar Remotely (Exclusive)

“When Sian first asked me, ‘Why do you want to do this?’ my answer truly was, “Because the movie fucking terrifies me,’” Walsh tells The Hollywood Reporter in support of Being Heumann’s Nov. 13 release on Apple TV.

In 1977, disabled rights activist Judy Heumann helped organize the landmark Section 504 Sit-in, a nationwide protest aimed at compelling HEW Secretary Joseph Califano to finally sign the long-delayed regulations implementing Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973. Heumann and her fellow disabled activists occupied federal buildings across the country for more than three weeks until Califano finally put pen to paper.

The regulations secured civil rights protections for disabled individuals and helped direct billions of dollars toward making federally funded infrastructure more accessible, including through curb cuts, wheelchair ramps, wider public restrooms and designated parking spaces. The movement also helped pave the way for the more sweeping Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990.

Walsh and Heder knew that if they were going to dramatize Heumann’s David-versus-Goliath tale, the only way to honor the late disabled pioneer was to bring her story to the screen authentically. That meant casting more than a dozen key roles with disabled actors and practicing what the movie preaches by creating an accessible, equitable set that could accommodate the ensemble’s unique needs.

The rub was that no such blueprint existed, and there was only one wheelchair-accessible trailer in all of North America. Working alongside a ten-person accessibility team and a crew that included disabled artisans and technicians, Walsh, Heder and their partners customized the Being Heumann set, taking extra precautions for the cast and ensuring direct access to personal and hair/makeup trailers.

“We did experience a handful of Califano-type people, just not from the studio side. Apple was great. It was more, You can’t do it this way. It’s never been done this way,” Walsh shares. “But we needed to ignore history and really try to recreate how people make movies. I’m as proud of what we did behind the scenes to redefine access as I am of the quality of this movie.”

Michael Patrick Thornton, who plays a supporting role opposite Ruth Madeley’s lead turn as Judy, put matters into perspective in a way Walsh will never forget. As one of the most accomplished disabled screen and stage actors of the last 25 years, Thornton found that Being Heumann offered him a first-time experience that most actors likely take for granted.

“On his first day, he got into the hair and makeup trailer and started to cry. He said, ‘In my whole career, I’ve never, ever seen the inside of a hair and makeup trailer,’” Walsh recalls. “He went on to describe it to me personally and said, ‘You don’t understand. This is Shangri-La for an actor who’s disabled. Normally, I’m in a closet getting ready on my own. But I feel like I’m one of everyone here.’”

Below, in a conversation with THR, the Manchester by the Sea producer also discusses his company’s prolific output in the 2020s, plus his extensive upcoming film and TV slate.

When we last spoke for Napoleon three years ago, the actors’ strike had just ended, and there were a lot of questions as to what the new normal would be. What did the answer end up being for you and The Walsh Company?

We’ve been lucky. We got to make three or four movies during the strikes, which was really something. We were able to keep shooting in Europe. Echo Valley did have to shut down because of the writers’ strike, so we went back to finish it. We then got a little independent film made called Miss You, Love You, and we’ve since made four films at Apple. Overall, we’ve now made five movies at Apple since [launching the Walsh Company and signing there in 2022]. So COVID and the strikes impacted us, but we were largely able to keep going.

Is it harder to set things up now? Or is it about the same?

It’s been about the same for us. We’ve been on a really good pace setting things up, but getting things made and securing that green light is always harder. The head of a streamer once joked, “Everybody’s been drinking at the bar for free, and now they’ve got to pay their tab.” So those days are gone when a streamer would green-light a $50 million to $70 million movie and say, “Hey, good luck.”

I have to really work for the green light now, but these streamers and studios need product. So I’m lucky to be in that small percentage of people who are still getting movies produced. We’ve set up a bunch of movies, and we’ve made five since we last talked. We’ve also started a TV business.

You and Sian Heder both have deals at Apple. Did they play matchmaker between the two of you for Being Heumann?

I actually met Sian during a party at Ben Affleck’s house. We both grew up outside of Boston, and we both expressed a desire to work together. I had been looking for the right thing, but Apple ultimately did play matchmaker because we both had deals there. They said they needed someone to come on alongside [producer] David Permut, who had identified the rights and done a great job developing the script. So Sian and I really bonded as we started to talk about the challenges of this movie, and I was excited to jump in with her.

You mentioned your fellow producer David Permut. Do you know the story of how he fended off Jean-Marc Vallée to acquire the rights to Judy Heumann’s story?

I don’t know the details surrounding the Jean-Marc of it all. I do know that David and Sian arrived at Judy separately, but then they quickly came together. I came in much later, but I was really happy to play a pivotal role in the development of the script and the execution of the movie.

Judy was at a decision-making point when Sian cold-emailed her [in 2020]. One of Sian’s best friends, who was an accessibility coordinator on Crip Camp, had told her to watch the documentary [co-starring Heumann]. Sian asked, “Why should I watch it?” And her friend said, “This woman needs to have a movie made about her.” So Sian watched Crip Camp, and she emailed Judy that same day to say, “Hey, I’m really interested in your story.” Judy wrote back 20 minutes later and said, “I’m making the decision on who I’m going to make this movie with today. So if you can get on the phone with me tonight at 5:00 p.m., you’ll be in the running.” Sian quickly finished her book and called her that night.

CODA came out in August 2021. It won the Oscar for best picture in March 2022. Sian’s follow-up is now out in November 2026. Was she indecisive about how she wanted to spend her Oscar capital? Or did it just take a while to get Being Heumann across the finish line?

I think she’s just really exacting. People misuse the word picky when exacting is the better word. She’s relentless in making sure something is really excellent, well done and well researched. So she took her time just to make sure it was the movie she wanted to commit to. She had a lot of opportunities with other films and studios, but they weren’t quite the right fit for her or an exact match with her DNA.

She really appreciates and supports underdogs — and this story certainly tells the ultimate underdog story. So it took time for her to get the script right, and then it took time for Apple to finally make that turn to say, “Okay, we’re going to make Being Heumann.” That’s just part of the normal process of getting movies green-lit.

I’m ashamed to admit I never fully realized how life-changing a curb cut could be for someone with a disability. And, as the movie points out, so many people were naive to that reality. But after watching Being Heumann, I’ve started noticing all the other forms of accessible infrastructure that Judy Heumann and her allies fought to establish.

You’re right that people don’t realize it. People do not realize how vital and how prevalent curbs cuts and other forms of barrier-free access are. Judy fought for them at a time when they didn’t exist. One of my favorite lines in the movie is about how anyone at any time can become a part of this subset of disabled people. We’ve done probably 15 Q&As over the last month, and you’d be surprised how many people are affected, whether it’s personally or through their siblings, their parents, their cousins, et cetera. This affects everyone. And if we’re lucky enough, we’ll live a long time — long enough to use a cane or a walker or a wheelchair.

Hollywood, meanwhile, still has very few figurative curb cuts for the disabled community, whether it’s telling their stories or hiring their performers. Did you encounter your own Joseph Califano types in trying to get this movie made?

We did experience a handful of Califano-type people, just not from the studio side. Apple was great. It was more, You can’t do it this way. It’s never been done this way. But we needed to ignore history in a way and really try to recreate how people make movies. I’m as proud of what we did behind the scenes to redefine access as I am of the quality of this movie.

Access is the word I keep coming back to for everything about this movie. We created a film set with access to trailers and ramps. We made sure that disabled people had access to every single thing that an able-bodied crew member had access to — and then some. That happened through a lot of hard work, ingenuity and research by our great team of people.

Did any wheelchair accessible Star Waggons exist?

There was one in all of North America. We actually ended up cutting the backs off some trailers and creating lifts to bring actors up into the hair and makeup trailer. We had a series of ramps built by our construction team and grips, which we laid out to lead actors to any trailers that weren’t accessible. It made such a difference.

One of our actors, Michael Patrick Thornton, who plays Ed Roberts, the self-described “artichoke” in the movie, had been working for 30 years in the movie business. He’s a huge Broadway actor and a big TV actor. He just finished a Broadway run with Keanu Reeves in [Waiting for Godot].

On his first day, he got into the hair and makeup trailer and started to cry. They asked him what was wrong, and he said, “In my whole career, I’ve never, ever seen the inside of a hair and makeup trailer.” I was so floored by that story and what we had done to achieve it. He went on to describe it to me personally and said, “You don’t understand. This is Shangri-La for an actor who’s disabled. Normally, I’m down the hall in a closet getting ready on my own. But I feel like I’m one of everyone here.” So, as a seasoned disabled actor, he could see the difference.

Was there extra crew to accommodate the disabled cast?

We had a 10-person accessibility team at all times. We provided masseuses, nutritionists and round-the-clock care. We had people transferring disabled actors from their regular wheelchairs to period wheelchairs. We’d give them time for stretches and breaks. We had a lot of disabled crew members working with us as well.

But we made a lot of mistakes throughout the process. We had to refine it and hone it and get it better and better. It was just really important for me to learn this new skillset. It’s one of the reasons why I did the movie. When Sian first asked me, “Why do you want to do this?” my answer truly was, “Because the movie fucking terrifies me.” I wanted to figure out all these issues. But with a good team around us, we were able to achieve it.

There are so many great disabled actors in this movie who had never acted before. They’d never been in a film before, much less a soundstage or a set. So, for them, it was like, This is how movies must work all the time. (Laughs.)

When it came to casting Judy and the other 504 protestors, how large was the talent pool of disabled actors?

You might be surprised to hear this, but there are a lot of really talented people. Our casting directors, Bernie Telsey and Adam Caldwell, really put the spotlight on that community. Had we not tried to authentically cast people with the actual disabilities of the characters they’re portraying, we wouldn’t have found that talent.

For Judy, it was a bit more specific. We had to find a disabled person who has the charisma and acting chops to lead a movie, but also possess the same kind of ferociousness and tenacity that Judy had. So there aren’t a lot of Ruth Madeleys out there.

Hopefully, this movie opens more doors for everyone.

Yeah, my hope is that people will shine a spotlight on these actors so that they’ll be considered for other parts. We’re developing a TV show right now for an A-list TV actress, and I’ve pitched one of our disabled actors, Andrew Pilkington, to play her sibling. He plays Hale Zukas in Being Heumann, and he communicates with the antenna on the board. So I just said, “How great would it be if he were the brother of this actress? That would provide a whole other layer of complexity to this show.”

I’m also doing the Team Hoyt movie at Netflix with producers Gotham Chopra and Tom Brady, and [directors] Nat Faxon and Jim Rash. I’m bringing Andrew Pilkington on because he’s a producer in his own right, and he’s going to help me with authenticity. We have an actor who has cerebral palsy, and he’ll oversee the way we make the movie.

So there is a lot of talent in front of the camera and behind it. It’s just a matter of redefining the norms of casting actors in movies and TV shows and learning to look at everyone all at once. Again, access.

One of the best performances of the year was given by a disabled actor named Steve Way on the series Furious, which was partially directed by Cory Finley, who you helped launch by way of Thoroughbreds.

Yes, Steve is incredible. Sian knows Steve. She chatted with him, but Steve had some conflicts regarding this movie. I just read in the trades a couple days ago that Ramy Youssef and Steve are doing a body swap comedy, which is really interesting. What Steve and Cory and [creator] Liz Meriwether did on that show is amazing. We’re actually getting ready to start prep on Cory’s next film. It’s coming up next year with a really good cast.

I admire how honestly Being Heumann portrays its disabled characters. They’re generally altruistic, but they still make mistakes and give in to their impulses, like we all do. In other words, the film doesn’t portray them as infallible saints simply because they’re disabled. Did the ensemble also appreciate this unvarnished take?

They totally did. I’m glad you mentioned that because one of the geniuses of Sian Heder is that she’s able to create an arc for all 15 of these characters. And I will say she proved me wrong. Early, early on, before prep, I said, “There’s too many people to service, Sian. I don’t know if you’re going to get around to all of it.” And she did. One of the most amazing feats of the movie is that each person you meet has their own little 180-degree turn. And so the actors loved that.

A lot of times, when we see disabled characters, they’re either perceived as saintly or bitter because they’re dealing with their disability, but they are like anybody else. They just happen to be in a wheelchair or unable to access certain things that non-disabled people have access to. So the actors really appreciated how layered and different all these characters were.

I was also impressed by how they let their personal experiences shine through in their characters quite a bit. If you recall the testimonials in the movie, Sian wisely guided and directed them to look inward a bit as they were telling those stories about their disabilities. That infused the film with a certain credibility, but also emotion.

Mark Ruffalo and Dylan O’Brien both fit their roles so well, but the cynical viewpoint is that you needed a couple names to appease the powers that be.

They just responded well to the material. Don’t get me wrong, it’s always beneficial to have movie stars help open a film and bring awareness to a film. But Apple was supporting this film through and through, head to toe. [Apple TV bosses] Zack Van Amburg, Jamie Erlicht, and Matt Dentler really got behind this movie and said, “Go make the film. Stick to this number, but go make the film.” So we didn’t need any real names. We were just lucky to get Mark and Dylan.

Mark is a once-in-a-generation-level actor. We’re working together on another project that he’s going to star in and direct. I spoke to him this morning in fact. He is perfect in the role of Califano. It’s a very complex, layered part. He could be perceived as a cold, simple villain, but he’s really a guy who’s just trying to do his best. And at the end of the day, he tips his hat to Judy, nicely, by saying, “Well fought.”

Dylan is another wonderful actor with a huge following, so we got lucky to have those guys help raise awareness of the film. But we didn’t really need them.

The postscript says that the fight for disability rights is far from over. Do you happen to know what the outstanding issues are?

Yeah, a lot of these Section 504 rights and regulations are now being conflated with the argument about transgender rights. They all fall under the same umbrella. So, in 14 states right now, they’re trying to repeal funding for some of these Section 504 rights because of other rights that fall under that umbrella. There was a big article about this in Time magazine within the last couple of months.

What people don’t understand is that you’re talking about taking away curb cuts, elevators and access for disabled people in our community. This is why it’s super important, and it saddens me that we’re still having this conversation 50 years later. If you’re against the idea of a person in a wheelchair being able to access a federal building, a post office or a place to get their passport renewed, you’re on the wrong side of history. It’s just that simple. So you have to look closely at what you’re reading, what you’re voting for and who you’re supporting.

I spoke to Tom Pelphrey and Louis Leterrier not too long ago, and your sci-fi action-thriller with them, Liminal, came up. What else are you excited about on the Walsh Company slate?

I’m really excited about Louis’ movie. He’s got a murderer’s row of great actors. Besides Tom, it has Vanessa Kirby, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Tracy Letts and Franka Potente. So we’re in post on that right now.

We’ve also had a rocket-ship start to our TV business. We hired an executive named Danny Feldheim about a year and a half ago, and we’ve set up ten TV shows in that time. We have five or six shows at Apple, a show with John Mulaney and Langston Kerman at HBO and another great show called The Hawk with Dave Collard and Casey Affleck at Hulu. So we’re excited about being all over that side of the business.

We’re also prepping three or four movies for next year. We just got something in the last week that I’m most excited about. There’s a Black List script called Best Seller that was with Peter Rice until he left to take the [Netflix CCO] job. We got lucky enough to meet on it, and while it went out to 10 or 15 producers, we won that movie. So we’re really excited about putting it together and getting a director on it.

We’re finally going to make Adam and Aaron Nee’s next movie, Calamity Hustle, next year. We’re getting close on that deal with two actors.

Ryan Reynolds and Channing Tatum are no longer attached?

It’s no longer Ryan and Channing. It’s going to be a couple other actors, but we’re really excited about it. The Nee brothers have done a really good job on the script, and they’re ready to go. They’ve said no to a lot of movies to make this movie.

You mentioned it earlier, but what’s the latest on Cory Finley’s next one?

Yeah, we’re going to make Cory’s upcoming film [Reasonable People] with Paul Rudd and Sam Rockwell, which will probably be a fall shoot. We’re out to another actor now, and we’re closing a deal with a really exciting financier who’s going to do it. It’s a wonderful story about revenge in modern-day America. It’s kind of like a present-day Hatfields & McCoys set in the suburbs. It has that same darkly comedic tone as Thoroughbreds, with really nuanced characters and a deep dive into the relationship between two fathers and one of the fathers’ brothers in this suburban community.

Then we have a really big film at Apple that we’re getting quite close on for next year. It’s a Christmas movie. So it could be a busy year next year, but I’m honestly just lucky and happy to be making movies and doing what I love. Apple has been great to us, and I’m grateful they’ve given us a platform.

“Obsession and Backrooms” has been the most repeated phrase this year. Everyone’s been trying to discern what the takeaway should be. Rather than simply hiring more YouTubers or adapting unusual internet properties, is the real lesson to take chances on newer, original voices, regardless of platform or genre?

You’re right about original voices. Matisse Haddad, who wrote Best Seller, is an original voice. It’s one of her early screenplays, and it’s one of the best scripts I’ve read in a long time. There’s another great young writer named Cody Brotter who’s writing the Bon Jovi story for us at Universal. He has a Black List script called Drudge about Matt Drudge, which is also one of the best scripts I’ve ever read. We’re going to try to get that made.

So it’s about finding young voices and just trusting youthful filmmakers. There’s a great script we love called The Toe by a writer named Mallory Westfall. It’s completely bonkers and left of center and dark, but original and great and unlike anything you’ll read. It’s harder to make those kinds of movies. Those [tonal seesaws], like Cory’s next movie, are harder lifts, but you’re fighting for originality at the end of the day.

There are filmmakers to be found on YouTube, just like there’s filmmakers to be found everywhere. It’s just about keeping an open mind to originality and setting your own pace and not trying to copy something else. The directive at our company isn’t, Go find us an action movie or a romantic comedy. It’s always, What makes you sit up straight when you read it? Do you want to make it and why? That’s really all we look for.

We’ve reached the dreaded AI question. Initially, the creative community drew a hard line in the sand against its use. But now there’s filmmakers like Doug Liman and Darren Aronofsky who are experimenting with it rather aggressively, while directors like Ben Affleck, Danny Boyle, and Ava DuVernay have acknowledged using it for minor details, such as animating old photographs. But as the scope keeps creeping outward, those minor details could soon become major ones, and entire departments could be gutted or downsized in no time. Maybe I’m being an alarmist, but do you think it’s inevitable at this rate?

I don’t think you’re being alarmist, but I don’t think it’s inevitable, either. There’s always going to be human artistry that you need to harness.

Some people say, “Graphic designers and previs artists and other visual artists are going to be gone.” John P. Goldsmith, who was my production designer on Being Heumann, has a degree from Harvard — a master’s in architecture. He did Boston Strangler with me. He’s a genius. On Being Heumann, he designed all the detailed lobby work, like the brass elevator buttons and the marbling, in the building the protestors storm. All of that was constructed from scratch. John took all of his education, his history, his experience, all of it, and made sure that it looks right. People from Apple came to visit the set, and they couldn’t believe it.

It hearkens back to one of my first films in my early 20s when I worked as an assistant on The Hours. We dropped a shot while filming at a hotel in the south of London, and we moved back to the stage. We didn’t want to go back to the hotel location. So, Stephen Daldry, I believe, described the [dropped] shot to the production designer and the construction team. The next morning, I came back to the stage at Pinewood, and the hallway of this hotel had been reconstructed. It was flawless. I walked through it, and I couldn’t believe how exact a match it was. We put the actors in the hallway, Julianne Moore, and we had the shot.

So, yes, there’s a way to use AI quite a bit in previs, in post and with VFX, but you still need to harness that type of human creativity. You’re going to use AI as a tool. The filmmakers you mentioned — Danny, Ava and Ben — they’re using it as a tool in a great way. But if you ask any one of them, “Can you do away with human artistry and do your job?” they’d say that you can’t. This is a community medium. You need to have a team that executes at a high level. I could not make Being Heumann without my producing team of Sian, David, Kevin Cleary and John Beach.

We are using AI, for sure, with certain VFX stuff. There’s definitely some AI in the previs on bigger movies. But I came up working in a lot of different departments in moviemaking, and you will always need to harness artistic creativity. Without it, you’re going to have a movie that feels devoid of spirit. It’s going to look mechanical, and audiences are going to sniff it out.

Screenwriting, storytelling and directing need to keep redefining. Those areas can’t be iterative. If you’re going to be iterative with AI, you’ll just be rehashing old movies and old stories. So you need human creativity to explore other areas, and that’s where you’ll find your Backrooms and Being Heumanns, movies that have not been done before.

I’ve asked this question off and on over the years, but I Play Rocky has given me permission to dust it off. I love narrative features about the making of beloved movies. So out of all your projects, which one warrants the I Play Rocky treatment?

Oh man, that’s such a hard question. I had such a good time on The Way, Way Back. It was an incredible movie. I actually attended an AMPAS lunch this past weekend, and coincidentally, I was seated next to Mark Ricker, my production designer, on that movie. We talked about how it was his favorite movie ever.

Everyone rented beach houses alongside each other. Toni Collette, Allison Janney, Steve Carell, Sam Rockwell, Maya Rudolph and the rest of our wonderful cast all lived on the beach together. We would walk to work every day, shoot the movie and come home. That was a great moviemaking experience for the comedy of it, because [co-directors] Nat [Faxon] and Jim [Rash] and I would go to dinners and get cocktails with all our wonderful comedic actors each night. So there’s definitely a behind-the-scenes element to that.

But then there’s the scope and scale of the Ridley movies and those experiences. Napoleon was jaw-dropping to film and create. Seeing the scope of it made me pinch myself quite a few times and think, How did I get here? How did I get here from making a tiny little independent film 28 years earlier?

Would [script doctor] Paul Thomas Anderson be the second or third-act twist in the Napoleon making-of movie?

(Laughs.) Yes, the Paul part of that process was great and really rewarding to watch. I actually got to meet Paul much, much earlier than that. [Writer’s Note: In the early 2010s, Walsh attended a wedding officiated by Anderson. The filmmaker was so taken with Walsh’s look that he cast him in The Master.]

Then I would say House of Gucci, just with the legendary cast and the postcard-like tour of Italy. We made the movie in Rome, Milan, Lake Como and the Alps. I got to watch Al Pacino, Jeremy Irons, Gaga, Adam Driver and Jared Leto. It was a wonderful front-row seat to moviemaking with Ridley at the helm. He’s one of a kind.

***Being Heumann is now streaming on Apple TV.

#784. Journey Drummer Deen Castronovo Exits Mid-Tour to Focus on His Health

Steve Murphy will fill in for the rest of November, weeks after Castronovo suffered an onstage medical emergency in Tulsa.

Journey drummer Deen Castronovo is stepping away from the band’s farewell tour to deal with his health, the group announced Friday (Nov. 13).

“After careful consideration and an extensive year of touring, our talented, longtime drummer Deen Castronovo has decided to step away to focus on personal health matters that require his attention,” the band said in a statement. “He has our full support during this time and extends his heartfelt thanks to the fans for the love, encouragement, and kindness he has received.”

Steve Murphy will take over for the remainder of November. The New York drummer has previously worked with the Alan Parsons Project, Trans-Siberian Orchestra, Christopher Cross and Jack Bruce. Related John Summit, David Guetta, Alison Wonderland & More to Play College Football Playoff National Championship Weekend Young Thug Responds to Quavo's Attempt to Have Him Reconcile With Gunna: 'How Uma Fix Some Sh-- I Didn't Break Qua?' Who Is Sara Schell, The Newcomer Who Won Songwriter of the Year at the 2026 Latin Grammys? Explore Journey See latest videos, charts and news

The announcement follows a scare last month, when Castronovo was helped offstage and taken to hospital after two songs at Tulsa’s BOK Center on Oct. 8. He returned two nights later for a full show in San Antonio, and guitarist Neal Schon said at the time that he was “back in rare form.” Neither the band nor Castronovo has disclosed details of the illness.

Castronovo, 62, first joined Journey in 1998, replacing Steve Smith, and played on five albums before leaving in 2015. He returned in 2021, initially alongside Narada Michael Walden, and became the sole drummer after Walden’s 2022 departure. He also sings, occasionally taking lead vocals, and has played with Bad English, Hardline and Ozzy Osbourne.

His exit comes near the end of a long year on the road. The Final Frontier tour, promoted by AEG Presents, launched Feb. 28 in Hershey, Pa., with an initial 60 North American dates, before the band added 40 more for the fall. The current leg began Sept. 12 in Los Angeles. Keyboardist Jonathan Cain has said the run marks his own farewell chapter with the band, which also features founder Neal Schon, singer Arnel Pineda, keyboardist Jason Derlatka and bassist Todd Jensen.

The tour continues Saturday (Nov. 14) at Bon Secours Wellness Arena in Greenville, S.C., and wraps Nov. 28 at San Francisco’s Chase Center.

Journey’s commercial peak came with 1981’s Escape, the band’s only No. 1 album on the Billboard 200. It produced four Hot 100 hits, including “Open Arms,” their highest-charting single at No. 2, “Who’s Crying Now” at No. 4 and “Don’t Stop Believin’” at No. 9 — a song that long outlasted its chart run to become the band’s signature.

#783. Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders

Sleep disorders may have consequences that extend far beyond fatigue. New research from Florida International University (FIU) has found that several types of sleep disorders are associated with physical changes in brain regions responsible for attention, motivation, and decision-making. These findings suggest that disrupted sleep may be connected to important differences in the brain's structure.

Published in the journal Scientific Reports, the research offers one of the broadest examinations yet of the brain changes associated with different sleep disorders. The discoveries could eventually help scientists identify sleep problems earlier and develop treatments tailored to the specific brain systems involved.

What 57 Brain Imaging Studies Reveal About Sleep Disorders

An estimated 50 million to 70 million Americans experience sleep disorders, making them a major public health concern. To investigate their effects on the brain, scientists at FIU's Center for Children and Families combined and analyzed findings from 57 studies that used brain imaging to examine adults.

Rather than focusing on a single condition, the researchers compared several sleep disorders to determine whether they were associated with similar changes in brain structure. This approach, which is still relatively uncommon in sleep research, also allowed the team to identify differences specific to certain disorders.

The analysis focused on two broad groups. The first, known as dyssomnias, includes insomnia and sleep apnea, conditions that interfere with falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sufficient restorative sleep. The second group, called parasomnias, includes sleepwalking, nightmare disorder, and sleep terrors. These conditions involve unusual events or behaviors that interrupt normal sleep cycles.

"As more people recognize how important sleep is, there's growing urgency to understand what's happening in the brain," said Matthew Sutherland, a cognitive neuroscientist at FIU and senior author of the study. "By bringing together results from many studies, this research gives us a clearer picture of how sleep disorders affect brain structure and function and where we need to focus next."

Sleep Disorders Share Changes in a Critical Brain Region

One of the most striking findings was that both groups of sleep disorders were associated with reductions in the thalamus, a structure deep within the brain that plays a central role in processing information, sustaining attention, and supporting complex thinking.

The researchers identified changes in a specific part of the thalamus called the pulvinar. This region helps the brain direct attention toward important information and manage cognitive control, which allows people to regulate their thoughts and actions while completing tasks.

The affected areas are connected to larger brain networks that help people concentrate, make decisions, and respond to their surroundings. Differences in these systems may help explain why people with sleep disorders often experience slower reaction times, difficulty making decisions, and a greater likelihood of errors or accidents.

"Most research looks at sleep disorders one at a time," said Katharine Crooks, a recent FIU cognitive neuroscience doctoral graduate and lead author of the study. "By looking across many studies, we found shared patterns in the brain that help explain why sleep problems can impact focus, decision-making and everyday functioning. With so many people struggling with sleep, understanding what is happening in the brain is key to finding better interventions, diagnostic tools and personalized treatments."

Sleepwalking and Nightmares Show Additional Brain Differences

Although the researchers discovered common structural patterns across sleep disorders, they also found differences associated specifically with parasomnias.

People with these conditions showed changes in the posterior cingulate cortex, a brain region involved in motivation, decision-making, and the regulation of emotions. This finding may help explain why disorders such as sleepwalking, recurring nightmares, and sleep terrors can sometimes be accompanied by difficulties with mood, behavior, or emotional control.

In contrast, the analysis did not reveal a consistent pattern of structural changes found exclusively in dyssomnias, the category that includes insomnia and sleep apnea.

Together, these results suggest that different forms of disrupted sleep may be associated with both shared and distinct changes in the brain. The particular regions involved may depend on the nature of the sleep disorder.

Could Brain Imaging Lead to Better Sleep Disorder Treatments?

The findings provide researchers with new clues about the relationship between sleep disorders and the brain systems that support everyday thinking and behavior.

By identifying which regions are associated with particular sleep problems, scientists hope to improve diagnostic methods and develop more personalized interventions. Future treatments could potentially aim not only to improve sleep quality but also to protect the brain networks involved in attention, decision-making, and emotional regulation.

However, an important question remains unanswered. The research identified associations between sleep disorders and differences in brain structure, but it did not establish whether disrupted sleep causes those differences, whether existing brain differences contribute to sleep disorders, or whether both processes occur.

To investigate this relationship further, the FIU team plans to examine individual parasomnias in greater detail, including sleepwalking and REM sleep behavior disorder.

Understanding how these conditions relate to changes in the brain could help researchers develop better ways to recognize, manage, and potentially prevent some of the cognitive and emotional difficulties associated with disrupted sleep.

Materials provided by Florida International University. Original written by Rosanna Castro. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet.

NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth.

The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028.

The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples.

NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars, as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself.

Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet.

NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment.

However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame.

Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion.

How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column.

In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods?

Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington.

Jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc.

That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com.

"The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," said Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said.

During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as:

Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission.

According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module.

Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan.

China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. #781. Ben Stiller Gives Update on His New York Knicks Documentary: “The Pressure Is on”

The actor tells The Hollywood Reporter that the multi-part doc, in development with HBO and A24, will explore the team's history and championship run.

Ben Stiller is sharing an update on his forthcoming New York Knicks documentary, and after the team’s historic championship earlier this year, he knows “the pressure is on.”

While premiering his next film, Focker-in-Law, slated for a Thanksgiving release, on Wednesday night in New York, Stiller teased the documentary to The Hollywood Reporter, describing it as a multi-part project exploring the Knicks’ history.

“It’s going to be a multi-part documentary about the history of the Knicks, including this team. It’s about what they’ve been to New York and hopefully capture the spirit of the team,” he said. Related Stories Movies Elizabeth Holmes' Husband Billy Evans Claims He Didn't Consent to 'You Can See Everything' Nude Shower Scene Movies Margot Robbie to Star in A24's 'The Week of Pain' From 'The Drama' Filmmaker Kristoffer Borgli

“It’s been fun to work on so far,” Stiller added, acknowledging the high expectations surrounding the project, especially after the Knicks won their first NBA championship since 1973 on June 13. The documentary was announced shortly afterward, with Stiller directing the project and following the team’s full arc from the ’90s to its record-breaking championship run this year.

“I feel like Knicks fans really love the Knicks, so the pressure is on to make something that lives up to what they want, but I hope it does,” Stiller said.

As for where the project currently stands, Stiller said it is “in the beginning stages since the playoffs,” adding, “but it’s not gonna be long. We’re full on it.”

Stiller, who was born and raised in New York City, has been a lifelong Knicks fan, dating back to his childhood in the early 1970s. He’s also a staple star to sit courtside at games, alongside other celebrity fans including Timothée Chalamet, Spike Lee, Tracy Morgan, Tina Fey and more.

When asked if any of those superfans, specifically Chalamet, would appear in the documentary, Stiller said, “Yeah, there definitely are Knicks fans, both known and not known Knicks fans, because I love the community, fans in New York, all over New York, such a huge part of what it means to love the Knicks. So that community is really strong.”

Speculation that Stiller is working on a documentary about the NBA team grew after he was spotted filming content during the Knicks’ 2026 Finals run.

Immediately after Game 5 of the 2026 NBA Finals, cameras caught up with Stiller, and the Severance executive producer said he was “as happy as I’ve ever felt.”

Stiller joked with THR that he would check the score of the Knicks’ Wednesday night game against the Cleveland Cavaliers “right after” finishing interviews at the Focker-in-Law premiere and “periodically” throughout the film’s screening following the red carpet. However, the Knicks lost 115-107. Following the loss, Stiller wrote on X, “What happened.”

The Knicks are set to face the Indiana Pacers on Friday night in Indianapolis.

The past year has been... a lot. Record-breaking temperatures, devastating floods and catastrophic wildfires have brought the realities of climate change into sharp focus for people around the world. At the same time, many governments and organisations have scaled back on their climate action.

If you’re anything like me you might be feeling it’s all a bit ‘doom and gloom’. So in this series I decided to face my climate anxiety head on and set out in search of reasons for optimism.

In this first episode of Cooked? I talk to experts around the world about what the data really show and why there are still reasons to hope.

00:00 How climate change feels overwhelming

21:49 How are the world’s nations doing on climate change?

Nature: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5 °C climate target
